definition: Itinerant means traveling from place to place, especially for work.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word itinerant. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know itinerant should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: For thirty years the island churches shared one itinerant organist, who crossed with the Tuesday ferry and played six services in four days.
Traveling is weaker than itinerant: anyone on a single trip is traveling, while an itinerant worker goes further, making constant movement from place to place the shape of a working life.
Rootless goes past itinerant — the itinerant worker keeps a route and is awaited somewhere next Tuesday; the rootless have no route, no rounds, and nowhere they are due.

Peripatetic is the bookish cousin of itinerant — Aristotle's students learned while strolling, and the word still smiles a little at a life spent moving from post to post. Itinerant is the plainer working word, the one histories use for judges, preachers, and laborers on a circuit.

Nomadic describes a whole way of life that moves — herders and households shifting camp with the seasons, home and all. Itinerant is narrower and about work: the itinerant farrier or judge makes a living by rounds, while the home, if there is one, stays put.

The farrier's truck is a forge on wheels, and her week is a wheel too: Monday the racing yard in the valley, Wednesday the trail-riding outfit up the pass, Friday whichever small barns have called in.
Horses need shoeing where horses live, so the anvil goes to them.
She has no shop, no storefront, no fixed address between dawn and dark — an itinerant smith with no shortage of appointments, ever.
Itinerant is the exact word for that working life, because it means traveling from place to place, especially for work.
It is the opposite of drifting: her route is planned to the hour and every stop expects her.
What the word rules out is not order but a fixed workplace — the work itself is what moves.
Itinerant dignifies a working life on the move — itinerant judges, preachers, laborers — and histories lean on it.
It implies a circuit, not aimlessness: for roaming with no route at all, rootless or drifting is honest.
Keep it apart from this unit's migrate: migration is a population's move between regions with the seasons, while the itinerant worker makes a living by rounds, in any season.
And mind the sound-alike itinerary, which is the paper, not the person.

Before every village had screens, the movie came to you.
An itinerant projectionist would rattle into town with a truck, a generator, and a bedsheet-sized screen rolled up behind the cab.
His year was a circuit: the same two hundred villages in the same order, timed so each saw him just after harvest, when families had a little money.
Elders in parts of rural India still remember the sound of the generator as the signal that the show had arrived.
The projectionist kept a house he saw perhaps one month a year — the work moved constantly, even though the home never did.
